searches.note: Twenty eight searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's. Eight were restricted to a primary body's own domain and are read as primary through their summaries: ripaille.fr three times (once with the departmental tourist board), renardat-fache.com once, inao.gouv.fr with Légifrance and the ministry's bulletin four times (the Savoie cahier and Arbin, Roussette de Savoie, Marestel, Bugey Cerdon) and once more for the decree of 1973. Three searches found nothing (Ripaille's red by name, Magnin's making in English, Marestel's soils) and are counted. The search on the Savoie decree of 1973 served Ripaille's label and Magnin's story and is counted once, under Magnin. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept in a record marked checked.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the bodies' own pages (the INAO, Légifrance, the château of Ripaille, Renardat-Fâche) for their own dates, rules and methods, then to the open web for the second source of each date, person and place.

Where two sources disagreed on a year or a figure (the charterhouse, the successor at the Ardoisières, the end of Magnin, the Cerdon blend) the record gives what both allow; where a detail rested on one source or none (the transfer of Cerdon, mica schist, older barrels, Erythrite, the foundation's year) it was cut.

Sources whose title or address names a living person, or that are a person's own site, were read in the results and never cited: an importer of Ripaille whose address carries his name, a personal travel site, the regional magazine's long address that names a living chef (its short address is cited), the departmental tourist board's page whose address names the father of Renardat-Fâche, and two publishers named for living founders, which the refuter replaced (the guide in Dupasquier, the importer in Renardat-Fâche).

tested: The cru and its grape: a search of the Savoie cahier's texts (the homologations of 2015 and 2023 through the ministry's bulletin and the INAO extranet) lists Ripaille among the complementary names; secondary accounts give at least 80 per cent Chasselas for Crépy, Marignan, Marin and Ripaille, which was not read in the decree itself; the château's wine page calls its white an AOC Chasselas. The principal grape stands, and the record never says the cru is Chasselas alone.
The soil: the château's wine page gives glacial formations that make a gravelly, permeable soil, softened by Lake Geneva: confirmed, and the glacial origin added on the house's own page.

The making: an importer's page (steel, all of it through the malolactic) and a technical sheet (night picking, pressing, fermentation in steel tanks at a low temperature, the malolactic, a light filtration): steel and the malolactic stand on two, so the hedge to one importer goes.

Amédée VIII: the Dictionnaire historique de la Suisse (born 1383; in 1434 withdrawn to his residence of Ripaille made a hermitage, his son lieutenant general; elected by the Council of Basel in 1439; abdicated at Lausanne on 7 April 1449; died on 7 January 1451), with Hérodote and two Catholic encyclopedias on Felix V: confirmed. The day of the election differs (30 October or 5 November 1439), and the record gives the year only.

The first residence of about 1370: a heritage timeline gives Bonne de Bourbon's building there from 1371 to 1388 and the priory founded by Amédée VIII in 1410: the château's account stands as written, the Count and his wife described.

The Carthusians: 1623 on the château's own history page (through the efforts of Saint Francis de Sales, in the former priory) and in a study of Carthusian houses (founded 1623, incorporated by the general chapter of 1633); one château leaflet gives 1622; closed at the Revolution (1792 or 1793): changed to 1623 and the Revolution, the canons cut.

The purchase of 1892: the château's visit guide (sold by the heirs of General Dupas to the head of the DMC mills) and a visitor's account (in ruins in 1892); other pages of the château give about 1900 and the works ended in 1903: 1892 stands.
The foundation: its own page says the industrialist's granddaughter created it and gave it the castle; 1976 was in no source, and a search for it returned nothing: the year cut.
Faire ripaille: the Dictionnaire historique de la Suisse gives the legend of Ripaille as a place of revelry; no source read ties the phrase to it, so it stays said to come from it, and is left open.

The red and the rosé: the departmental tourist board gives Comte Rouge of Pinot Noir and Les Demoiselles du Château of Gamay, sold at the château; the château's sales page lists a white, a rosé and a red: the names stand, the recent addition cut.
Vin de Savoie as an appellation contrôlée since 1973: Légifrance (the decree of 4 September 1973, repealed in 1998) and the INAO (recognised in 1957, confirmed in 1973): the label stands.

The house rules: the owning family and its oenologist never named; the château's own figures for vines and bottles a year and its old wine prices not used; no score; no judging superlative; British; no dash.

The questions: Chasselas against Jacquère, Altesse and Roussanne, and Felix V against an emperor, a doge and a patriarch: one right answer each, plausible distractors, the explanations teach the nearest wrong one. The cards: sound.

tested: Arbin for reds of Mondeuse alone: the decrees of 1998 and 2009 (Mondeuse N exclusivement for Arbin and Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte) and the cahier of 2021 (Arbin among the still reds): confirmed.
Vin de Savoie an appellation contrôlée by the decree of 4 September 1973: Légifrance (the decree named and repealed in 1998) and the INAO (recognised in 1957, confirmed in 1973): confirmed.

The house's end: Les Caves de Pyrène (the couple winding down, 2022 their final harvest, undated); iDealwine's profile of the Ardoisières (the six leased hectares of Arbin taken on in 2024); a forum (a new Mondeuse of the Ardoisières from the former Magnin vines): the end and the vines stand, 2022 rests on one source read and goes.
The third generation: Les Caves de Pyrène, beside the two merchants the author read: stands.
The vines: iDealwine and Vinatis (some eight hectares, mainly in Arbin near Montmélian); all the Mondeuse within Arbin is Les Caves de Pyrène's alone: reworded to the Mondeuse in Arbin.
The soil: iDealwine (mainly clay and limestone scree, naturally well drained): stands; the south south east aspect and the steepness in no source read: cut.

The making: a merchant (hand picked and destemmed, up to twelve days with punching down in the first days) and iDealwine (destemmed, six days in steel): the span and mainly steel stand; the small part in older barrels (one importer) cut; told in the past, since the house no longer makes wine.
Organic and biodynamic: Vinatis (organic certified from 2012, biodynamic from 2010) against the author's other merchants (2007 and 2009): the story stays undated, as written.
Grand Orgue as the Chignin-Bergeron and the Vieilles Vignes: forum threads and iDealwine's listings, with the author's importer: stand; Chignin-Bergeron Roussanne by the decrees.
The house rules: the couple never named, the house keeping its name; no price (the auction listings read for the cuvées only); nothing volatile left once the end is told as history.

The questions: the wine question's key stands, its explanation now names the nearest wrong option; the story question's key, 2022, rested on one merchant's report of a plan, so the question is now who took on the vines, with Dupasquier, Ripaille and a co-operative as distractors.

The slope: up to sixty per cent of schist, worked entirely by hand (one merchant), steep and windy with poor soils (another), biodynamic (both): confirmed; mica schist and shallow soil in no source read: changed to schist.
The barrel: twelve months with a quarter new barrels in one vintage, eighteen months in oak in another: a year or more stands; most of them used ones and the racking cut.
The terraces: the magazine (the walls and the traditional cellars falling to ruin, the founder replanting in terraces): stands.
The successor: 2003, 2005 and 2008 in the sources read, the majority his from 2010 with the founder retired: changed to the 2000s.
The Magnin vines: iDealwine (taken on in 2024): stands as the early 2020s.
Silice: iDealwine gives Silice 2022 as a Vin de France of Jacquère bought from Apremont and the Isère: out of the list of IGP wines.
Erythrite: a second importer lists it as a red with half whole bunches and says nothing of Arbin: cut from the other wines.
Argile Blanc as IGP Vin des Allobroges: a forum thread's title and merchants' listings: stands.

The questions: Altesse against Jacquère, Chasselas and Mondeuse Blanche, and Cevins against Arbin, Jongieux and Chignin: one right answer each, plausible, the explanations teach. The cards: the first now says schist.
The house rules: the founder, his successor and the mayor never named; the hectares in the sources (12, 16, 24) not used; no superlative (the importer's cult in a title not cited).

Au Commencement: the house's shop (Au Commencement 2023) and a product listing (a sparkling rosé of Gamay and Poulsard): changed; Vin de France and on its lees not found.

The questions: one fermentation against a second with sugar and yeast, gas pumped in and a dosage, and Bugey against Savoie, the Jura and Beaujolais: one right answer each, plausible, the explanations teach. The cards: sound.

swaps.proposed: louis-magnin, to a working house of Arbin (Domaine des Fils de Charles Trosset or Domaine Fabien Trosset), since Domaine Louis Magnin has wound down and its leased Arbin vines passed to the Ardoisières
swaps.why: The end of a house is history, which the record now tells truly (wound down in the early 2020s, the leased Arbin vines passed to the Ardoisières by 2024), and it does not unmake the house's place: iDealwine's profile calls Domaine Louis Magnin a house of Savoie not to be missed, merchants in Britain, Switzerland, France and America sold its Arbin Mondeuse, its bottles of the years before 2022 stay in cellars and on lists for a decade and more (a merchant writes up a Mondeuse of twenty one years), and its tie to the Ardoisières pick teaches where the vines went. The two candidates are less known in every source read, the author named them for the refuter to confirm, and no search of the refuter's share was left to source a whole new record on two sources for every fact; a swap now would trade a sourced record for an unsourced one. If the owner or the read-together agent wants only working houses, the candidate should be researched by an author with a share of its own, under the thin region rule.
